Enhancing biodegradability of industrial park wastewater by packing
carriers and limited aeration in the hydrolysis process
Ying An a, Mengyu Wang a, Zhen Zhou a, b, *, Xiao Sun c, Cheng Cheng a, Songmei Zhu a,

a b s t r a c t
This study aims to ameliorate effects of packing carriers, ﬁlling ratio, temperature and limited aeration on
hydrolysis performance in a chemical industrial park wastewater treatment plant. Illumina-MiSeq
sequencing was applied to compare microbial community structure between bioﬁlm attached on carriers
and activated sludge in a full-scale hydrolysis tank. Packing carriers intensiﬁed the plentifulness of
microbial community, enriched hydrolytic bacteria (Betaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, Sphingo-
bacteria, Clostridia, Bacteroidia), and enhanced biodegradability of organics in the wastewater. Rising
carriers ﬁlling ratio increased ﬁrst-order kinetic constant of hydrolysis from 0.015 to 0.080 h1, and
decreased fractions inert to hydrolysis. Rising temperature stimulated enzymatic activity for hydrolysis
with activation energy of 80.22 kJ/mol. Limited aeration further enriched hydrolytic bacteria, inhibited
sulfate-reducing bacteria and intensiﬁed biodegradability of organic substances. Variations of ﬂuorescent
organic substances and ammonia nitrogen release during hydrolysis conﬁrmed that hydrolysis was
strengthened by packing carriers, increasing ﬁlling ratio, enhancing temperature and introducing limited
aeration. Packing carriers and limited aeration were techno-economic methods for enhancing hydrolysis
performance in the chemical industrial park wastewater treatment plant by enriching hydrolytic bacteria
and stimulating their activities.

1. Introduction
There are more than 2500 provincial-level industrial parks in
China, which contribute more than 50% of the national gross do-
mestic product (Hu et al., 2019a) but discharge enormous industrial
wastewater simultaneously (Hu et al., 2019b) with characteristics
of omnigenous compositions and high concentration of pollutants
(Zhu et al., 2016). Moreover, these compositions are usually toxic
and non-biodegradable (Liu et al., 2019), and probable cannot be
entirely degraded (Ma et al., 2016). Several treatment methods
based on physical, chemical, physical-chemical, and biological
mechanism were used widely in the chemical industrial park
wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) (Hu et al., 2019b). The low-
cost and energy-saving biological treatment technology was high-
ly appreciated among them. Nevertheless, the performance of
removing refractory compounds with biological treatment is not
efﬁcient, resulting in the low organic compounds removal efﬁ-
ciency, poor carbon source for denitriﬁcation and low utilization
ratio of energy. Ultimately, the concentrations of chemical oxygen
demand (COD) and total nitrogen (TN) could not meet re-
quirements in “Discharge Standard of Pollutants for Municipal
Wastewater Treatment Plant of China (GB18918-2002)". Therefore,
it is indispensable to develop the treatment technology for certain
degradation-resistant organic pollutants to enhance their removal
efﬁciencies.
Hydrolysis process is often employed to enhance biodegrad-
ability of the industrial park wastewater, making it conducive to the

succedent biological treatment. However, the composition of in-
dustrial park wastewater is very complex, making conventional
hydrolysis
by suspended
sludge
under
anaerobic
conditions
certainly difﬁcult (Wu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016). Intensive
efforts have been conducted in recent years to enhance hydrolysis
efﬁciency, and are very helpful to give some enlightenment for
industrial park wastewater treatment. In some cases, carriers could
store up high concentrations of active biomass and enrich the
growth of hydrolytic bacteria, which are indispensable for the
recalcitrant organic compounds degradation (Gu et al., 2014; Huang
et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2019). Micro-aeration by introducing small
amounts of oxygen into a bioreactor to stimulate biological activ-
ities of both anaerobic and aerobic biomass (Botheju and Bakke,
2011; Kong et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014), has the potential to
accelerate hydrolysis. Wu et al. (2015) reported that the biochem-
ical oxygen demand (BOD5)/COD of the petrochemical wastewater
increased from 0.23 to 0.43 by limited aeration in the hydrolysis
tank. However, there was limited information on effects of carrier
and limited aeration on hydrolysis performance of industrial park
wastewater treatment. More detailed research is needed for the
combination of limited aeration and carriers in hydrolysis tanks,
which is a potentially effective strategy to enhance biodegradability
of industrial park wastewater.
In this study, carriers were ﬁrstly suspended in the hydrolysis
tank of an industrial park WWTP to incubate bioﬁlm attached on
their surfaces, and then used to investigate effects of ﬁlling ratio,
temperature and limited aeration on hydrolysis efﬁciency and
biodegradation of treated wastewater. Illumina-MiSeq sequencing
was applied to investigate the microbial community structure and
population composition of bioﬁlm and activated sludge (AS) in the
hydrolysis tank. The hydrolysis process was also evaluated by a
ﬁrst-order kinetic model. The dissolved organic matters (DOM) in
the industrial park wastewater were also characterized by the
three-dimensional excitation-emission matrix (3D-EEM) ﬂuores-
cence spectroscopy. The results of this study are expected to pro-
vide some feasible enhancement strategies on hydrolysis of
industrial park wastewater.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Activated sludge
AS used in this study was obtained from hydrolysis tank of a
chemical industrial park WWTP (Jiangsu, China) operated stable for
two years with wastewater ﬂow rate of 20,000 m3/d treated by
hydrolysis e anoxic/anaerobic/oxic (AAO) - sequencing batch
reactor (SBR) process. The hydraulic retention times (HRT) of hy-
drolysis, anoxic, anaerobic, oxic and SBR were 24, 4, 4, 12 and 4 h.
The wastewater treated by the chemical industrial park WWTP was
a mixed wastewater, including domestic wastewater, pharmaceu-
tical industry wastewater, petroleum industrial wastewater, textile
dye industry wastewater, etc. The main characteristics of samples
from the WWTP were as follows: pH of 7.5e8.5, soluble COD
(SCOD) of 112.8e158.2 mg/L, BOD5 of 6.8e16.2 mg/L, NH4þ-N of
8.5e11.0 mg/L, and TN of 29.9e40.5 mg/L.
2.2. Carriers for bioﬁlm attachment
The LEVAPOR biocarriers (LEVAPOR GmbH Bioﬁlm Technolo-
gies, Leverkusen, Germany), which were made from polyethylene
(PE) with total surface area of 20,000 m2/m3, were employed as
carriers for bioﬁlm attachment in this study. The bioﬁlm attached
on PE carriers was grown and incubated for three months in the
hydrolysis tank of the WWTP before conducting the batch tests.
Part of the PE carriers incubated for three months were taken out
and placed in a lab-scale hydrolysis reactor under the condition of
limited aeration for another 30 d, and the industrial park waste-
water was fed into the reactor to maintain HRT of 24 h.
2.3. Experimental procedure
In order to investigate effects of carrier ﬁlling ratio, temperature
and limited aeration on hydrolysis efﬁciency, some lab-scale re-
actors of 5 L equipped with immersion thermostat and magnetic
stirrer were designed. All reactors were initially seeded with the
same AS and carriers with bioﬁlm attached on their surfaces, and
then fed with inﬂuent of the WWTP to maintain COD concentration
at approximately 125e170 mg/L. The stirring rate was maintained
at 120 rpm to make AS and carriers mix homogenously. After start-
up, samples were taken from each reactor using a pipette at 0, 3, 9,
18, 28, 38 and 48 h for the immediately analysis of COD, BOD5 and
NH4þ-N concentrations in duplicate after ﬁltration by 0.45 mm vinyl
cellulose membranes. The ﬂuorescence characterization of DOM
collected at 0, 9, 28, and 48 h were also analyzed using the 3D-EEM
ﬂuorescence spectroscopy.
The operational conditions are shown in Table 1. Firstly, the ef-
fect of carrier ﬁlling ratio on hydrolysis was concurrently investi-
gated at three carrier ﬁlling ratios of 0, 30%, and 60% under
anaerobic condition. And the temperature was sustained at values
of 25 ± 0.1 C. Secondly, under anaerobic condition, the batch tests
of hydrolysis were also conducted at 15 ± 0.1, 25 ± 0.1 and
35 ± 0.1 C to investigate temperature effects at carrier ﬁlling ratio
of 30%. Lastly, two reactors were also operated in parallel under
anaerobic condition and the condition of limited aeration with
average dissolved oxygen (DO) of 0.2e0.5 mg/L. The carrier ﬁlling
ratio and temperature were controlled at 30% and 25 ± 0.1 C. All
the experiments were conducted in duplicate.
2.4. Microbial diversity analysis
Microbial community structure of an AS sample (from the full-
scale hydrolysis tank) and two bioﬁlm samples (from carriers sus-
pended in the hydrolysis tank for three months, and the hydrolysis
reactor under limited aeration for 30 days) were analyzed by MiSeq
sequencing to compare microbial community structure evolution.
The detailed experimental steps of DNA extraction, PCR ampliﬁ-
cation, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, biodiversity analysis and
phylogenetic classiﬁcation were all in accordance with the reported
methods described by An et al. (2017). Finally, sequencing produced
more than 34,000 high-quality V3eV4 tags for 16S rRNA genes with
an average length of 436 bp by setting a 0.03 distance limit (a). To
equitably compare the two samples at the same sequencing depth,
the sub.sample command of Mothur program was employed for
normalization, and 34,094 sequences were extracted from each
dataset. Based on cluster information, parameters referring to
species richness (Ace and Chao), community diversity (Shannon
and Simpson) and sequencing depth (Good’s Coverage) were
calculated by Mothur software.

2.6. Other item analysis and statistical analysis
Concentrations of COD, BOD5 and NH4þ-N in samples were
analyzed according to standard methods (Chinese NEPA, 2012). DO
concentration in the reactor was tested by an HQd30 m (HACH,
USA). The 3D-EEM ﬂuorescence spectra of the supernatant were
conducted using a ﬂuorospectrophotometer (RF-5301pc, Shi-
madzu, Japan). The parallel factor (PARAFAC) analysis was per-
formed for all EEM spectra in MATLAB R2013a (Mathworks, USA)
using the DOMFluor.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Microbial community
The integrated investigation of microbial community composi-
tion and diversity of AS and bioﬁlm attached on the surface of
carriers was performed through MiSeq sequencing before con-
ducting the batch tests. The purposes of this section were to show
microbial evolution of packing carriers and limited aeration in the
hydrolysis tank for industrial park wastewater treatment, and to
elucidate the composition of microorganisms involved in the
following batch tests.
3.1.1. Richness and diversity of bacteria phylotypes
The statistical results of diversity analysis (Table 2) showed that
the microbial community structure and composition in AS differed
from bioﬁlm, although the microorganisms in bioﬁlm originated
from AS in the hydrolysis tank. It is conjectured that microbial
growth may be different in the hydrolysis tank and on the surface of
PE carriers. By performing the alignment at an approximate 436 bp
length, 1077 (AS) and 1142 (bioﬁlm) operational taxonomic units
(OTUs) were clustered at a 0.03 cutoff level. The total OTUs esti-
mated through Chao’s estimation with inﬁnite sampling was 1112
(AS) and 1186 (bioﬁlm), indicating that bioﬁlm had higher micro-
bial richness than AS (Cheng et al., 2017). Higher Shannon value and
lower Simpson value demonstrated that microbial community of
bioﬁlm was more diverse in terms of distribution and evenness
than that of AS (Cheng et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2017). Moreover, the
higher Shannon index suggested that the enriched OTUs in bioﬁlm
community were distributed more evenly than that in AS (Ma et al.,
2013a). All four indices in Table 2 illustrated that bioﬁlm had higher
diversity than AS (Matar et al., 2017), indicating that PE carriers
provided better substrates for hydrolysis by disintegrating the ﬂoc
structure of AS. The Good’s coverage obtained for each sample was
both above 0.99, revealed that the sequences generated at this
sequencing depth could well represent the bacterial communities
of AS and bioﬁlm samples.
3.1.2. Bacterial taxonomic identiﬁcation
To identify the changes of bacterial community structure and
composition between AS and bioﬁlm, the phylogenetic spectrums
were employed to distinguish taxa levels from phylum to genus
(Fig. 1). Fig. 1a depicts the relative bacterial abundance on the
phylum taxonomic level. 42 bacterial phyla, demonstrating greatly
high diversity, were detected in microbial communities of the two
samples. The majority of the sequence reads were assigned to six
major phyla: Chloroﬂexi, Proteobacteria, Acidobacteria, Bacteroidetes,
Chlorobi and Gemmatimonadetes, which in total contributed to
80.8% (AS) and 84.8% (bioﬁlm) of the entire sequence reads,
respectively. Previous studies reported that these phyla were
ubiquitous in AS and bioﬁlms (Choi et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2013a; Xie
et al., 2014). The dominant microorganisms in bioﬁlm resembled
that of AS, indicating that the microorganisms derived from AS
might induce an effect of colonization on the surface of PE carriers.
However, the differentiation of percentages procured for each
phylum sample was also observed. For example, Chloroﬂexi, playing
a role in degrading carbohydrates and cellular materials (Choi et al.,
2017), was the most dominant phylum in AS, accounting for 35.8%
of the total sequence reads. While Proteobacteria replaced Chloro-
ﬂexi, and became the most dominant phylum in bioﬁlm (35.7%),
indicating that PE carriers promoted its growth. The total sequence
reads of Bacteroidetes in the bioﬁlm (8.4%) were higher than to
those in the AS (5.6%). In the anaerobic condition, Proteobacteria
could induce cell lysis and release intracellular substances, and
then Bacteroidetes utilized the secondary substrate for hydrolytic
fermentation to proliferate (Han et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009). Be-
sides, Firmicutes could be related to denitriﬁcation and complex
organic matters degradation (Kumar et al., 2010). The relative
abundance of Firmicutes, in particular Clostridium sp., having spores
to stand up to the unfavorable environment (Xie et al., 2014), was
1.0% in bioﬁlm, higher than that in AS (0.4%). After that, additional
research down to the class and genus level was performed to
recognize bacterial pioneers between AS and bioﬁlm.

Fig. 1b illustrates the class taxonomic level identiﬁcation of the
microbial communities. 89 bacterial classes were detected in these
two communities. However, the majority of sequences pertained to
18 classes (i.e., >1% relative abundance), which in total accounted
for 88.3% and 88.6% of the total phyla in AS and bioﬁlm, respec-
tively. Compared to those in AS, Betaproteobacteria (Proteobacteria),

community in the bioﬁlm. Anaerolineae of phylum Chloroﬂexi,
activated in the anaerobic biogas production processes (Wu et al.,
2016), was the most dominant class in AS (20.5%), whereas its
abundance decreased and became the second dominant class in
bioﬁlm (14.8%). On the contrary, the proportions of Beta-, Gamma-,
Alpha- and Deltaproteobacteria afﬁliated to phylum Proteobacteria,
which were responsible for polysaccharides utilization or butyric
acid fermentation (Niu et al., 2016), were all obviously higher in
bioﬁlm than those in AS. The relative abundance of Betaproteo-
bacteria was 11.3% in AS, but increased signiﬁcantly to 22.0% in
bioﬁlm. With this change, Betaproteobacteria became the most
dominant class in bioﬁlm. Similarly, the relative abundance of
Gemmatimonadetes and Sphingobacteriia, accounted for 3.9% and
4.7% of total sequences in AS, and increased to 6.3% and 5.7% in
bioﬁlm. Sphingobacteria was concerned with anaerobic hydrolysis
fermentation and secretion of extracellular enzymes (Zhou et al.,
2015). Besides, the relative abundances of Clostridia and Bacter-
oidia responsible for organic matters hydrolysis and fermentation
(Xie et al., 2014, 2016), were 0.9% and 0.02% in bioﬁlm, and higher
than those in AS (0.4% and 0.003%). ML635J-21 and SC3-20 were
detected in bioﬁlm while were not detectable in AS. These results

Fig. 1c demonstrates the genus taxonomic level identiﬁcation of
the microbial communities. AS and bioﬁlm had similar genera
compositions but different relative abundances for speciﬁc genus.
The genera Anaerolineaceae_uncultured (14.1e18.9%), Caldilinea-
ceae_uncultured (5.3e11.2%), Blastocatella (3.4e5.3%), Gemmatimo-
nadaceae_uncultured
(3.6e6.0%),
Rhodocyclaceae_uncultured
(3.6e7.2%) and Saprospiraceae_uncultured (2.8e3.3%) were domi-
nant in both AS and bioﬁlm. Anaerolineaceae, a semi-syntrophic and
fatty acid oxidizing bacteria, was considered to be responsible for
carbohydrate couples degradation with hydrogenotrophic metha-
nogens (Ding et al., 2016). Blastocatella of phylum Acidobacteria, the
chemoheterotrophic bacteria correlated with hydrolysis, were also
found to survive in the anaerobic side-stream reactor (Cheng et al.,
2017). Saprospiraceae_uncultured, belonging to phylum Bacter-
oidetes, could be capable of hydrolyzing carbon polymers and
preying of other bacteria (Cheng et al., 2018). Besides, some minor
genera, including Acidaminobacter, Fusibacter and Gelria, were
enriched in bioﬁlm, with relative abundance of 0.10%, 0.09% and
0.02%, rather than AS with relative abundance of 0.003%, 0.003%
and 0.01%. These genera were determined to be the protein- and
carbohydrate-fermenting bacteria reported previously by other
researchers (Chen and Chang, 2017). The genera Ramlibacter, only
present in bioﬁlm, was an anaerobic and or facultative anaerobic
bacterium reported to slowly grow by the reduction of oxyanions,
such as nitrite, nitrate, sulfate, and perchlorate (Zhou et al., 2014).
In summary, microorganisms accumulated on the surface of PE
carriers were mainly originated from AS, while the population
composition was changed (Ma et al., 2013b). Compared to those in
AS,
Betaproteobacteria,
Gammaproteobacteria,
Sphingobacteria,
Clostridia and Bacteroidia, which could play an important role in
biological hydrolysis of organic matters, were found to be the pi-
oneers involved in the surface colonization on the PE carriers.
3.2. Kinetics of organic substances hydrolysis
Fig. 2 shows effects of carrier ﬁlling ratio, temperature and
limited aeration on COD removal in the hydrolysis process. Varia-
tions of COD concentration in the supernatant with time in Fig. 2
were ﬁtted by Eq. (2), and the results are illustrated in Table 3.
Higher coefﬁcients of determination in the ﬁt curve mean higher
credibility to the ﬁrst-order kinetics. Hydrolysis not only increased
COD removal, but also intensiﬁed biodegradability of organic sub-
stances in wastewater. Fig. 3 demonstrates effects of carrier ﬁlling
ratio, temperature and limited aeration on BOD5/COD ratio in the
hydrolysis process.
3.2.1. Effects of carriers ﬁlling ratio
As shown in Fig. 2a, there was an obvious downtrend in the COD
concentration with the increase of the carrier ﬁlling ratio in hy-
drolysis process. At the end of the reaction (48 h), SCOD concen-
trations in the supernatant were 134.0, 105.3, and 94.2 mg/L at
ﬁlling ratio of 0, 30% and 60%, respectively. Higher carrier ﬁlling
ratio provided more biomass for hydrolysis, and resulted in better
COD removal efﬁciency (Gu et al., 2014). The COD biodegradation
process appeared to follow the ﬁrst-order kinetic, and the
biodegradation rate depended on the carrier ﬁlling ratio. With
carrier ﬁlling ratio rising from 0 to 60% (Table 3), k increased 0.015
to 0.080 h1, while the inert fraction CODI decreased from 119.5 to
94.0 mg COD/L. It could be explained that packing PE carriers
increased the population and abundance of microorganisms and

enhanced the ability of organic matter degradation, so more re-

At the beginning, the BOD5/COD ratio in the supernatant of raw
wastewater was only 0.11, and elevated to 0.20 and 0.29 after hy-
drolysis for 24 and 48 h without carriers, indicating that biological
treatment process was inappropriate even after hydrolysis. How-
ever, the ratio signiﬁcantly could augment to 0.42 and 0.54 after
hydrolysis for 48 h with carriers ﬁlling ratio of 30% and 60%
(Fig. 3a). The results indicated that packing carriers could improve
the biodegradability of the industrial park wastewater, and
increasing
ﬁlling
ratio
further
enhanced
biodegradability
of
unbiodegradable organic pollutants and favored COD removal in
the succedent biological process.
3.2.2. Effects of temperature
Temperature is an important factor affecting a large number of
biological processes (Li et al., 2015), including hydrolysis (He et al.,
2012). According to Fig. 2b, with the temperature increment from
15 C to 25 C and 35 C, the COD removal efﬁciencies increased
continuously and reached 13.3%, 39.8%, and 43.6% after 48 h hy-
drolysis, respectively. Obviously, higher temperature achieved
relative higher COD removal efﬁciency by promoting metabolism
rate to enhance COD removal (Li et al., 2015). Compared with car-
rier ﬁlling ratio, similar variation trends of k and CODI with tem-
perature could also be observed (Table 3). When the temperature
was adjusted from 15 C to 35 C, k was signiﬁcantly increased from
0.015 to 0.130 h1, while CODI was reduced from 128.1 to 100.9 mg
COD/L. It was shown that increasing the temperature enhanced
enzymatic activity for hydrolysis, and the inﬂuence of temperature
on k can be described by Arrhenius equation (Tian et al., 2019). The
Ea of hydrolysis process with carriers for COD removal from in-
dustrial park wastewater was calculated to be 80.22 kJ/mol, which
was slightly greater than the typical value for enzyme kinetics re-
action (20e80 kJ/mol) (Zhang et al., 2016).
Temperature can greatly inﬂuence the thermodynamic equi-
librium of biochemical reactions and microbial community in the
biological hydrolysis process (Lin et al., 2016, 2017). For example,
Betaproteobacteria and Clostridia showed evidently increased per-
centages with the increment in temperature (Chen and Chang,
2017), reﬂecting that the growth of the functional hydrolysis bac-
teria was elevated with rising temperature. The BOD5/COD ratio
obtained with time at different temperatures were given in Fig. 3b.
The BOD5/COD ratio increased to 0.27, 0.42 and 0.66 after 48 h
hydrolysis with carriers at ﬁlling ratio of 30% at 15, 25 and 35 C,
respectively. The results indicated that increasing temperature
beneﬁted to enhancing biodegradability. It should be noted that,
the biodegradability of organic substance in the industrial park
wastewater was slightly improved under low temperature even
after packing carriers, which would obstacle COD removal in
winter. Heating and insulation measures are proposed to be
employed for the hydrolysis unit if waste heat could be provided in
the industrial park.

3.2.3. Effects of limited aeration
It can be perceived that limited aeration is an environmentally
friendly, rapid and safe technology for the hydrolysis pretreatment
of a mixed wastewater (Wu et al., 2015), including domestic
wastewater, pharmaceutical industry wastewater, petroleum in-
dustrial wastewater, textile dye industry wastewater, etc. As illus-
trated in Fig. 2c, the COD removal rate in the limited aeration
reactor (43.8%) was higher than that in the anaerobic reactor
without aeration (28.3%). As for kinetics, limited aeration enhanced
parameter k by 80.8%, and reduced CODI from 87.7 mg COD/L to
73.5 mg COD/L. The results indicated that limited aeration accel-
erate hydrolysis of complex organic matters by stimulating bio-
logical activities of both anaerobic and aerobic organisms (Niu et al.,
2016).
As shown in Fig. 3c, limited aeration also enhanced biodegrad-
ability as BOD5/COD ratio rose from 0.46 to 0.61 after 48 h hydro-
lysis with carriers at ﬁlling ratio of 30%. Besides stimulating
hydrolytic activity, limited aeration also prohibited the consump-
tion of biodegradable BOD in the sulfate reduction process. Illu-
mina-MiSeq sequencing results showed that the predominant
microorganisms in bioﬁlm of the limited aeration reactor and the
anaerobic reactor exhibited a high homology (Fig. 1). According to
Wu et al. (2015), low DO condition (0.2e0.3 mg/L) could weak or
block SO42 reduction to a certain degree in the hydrolysis acidiﬁ-
cation process, ultimately resulting in the less generation of H2S
and fewer consumption of BOD. That could improve the biodeg-
radation and treatability for the hydrolysis process. It should be
noted that (Fig. 1c) the total abundance of the sulfate-reducing
bacteria Desulfobacula, Desulfobulbus, Desulfocapsa, Desulfococcus,
Desulfofustis,
Desulfomicrobium,
Desulforhabdus,
Desulfovibrio,
Desulfurispora, and Desulfuromonas, which could reduce sulfate to
hydrogen sulﬁde by using organic matters, were detected in bioﬁlm
of the limited aeration reactor (0.42%) and lower than that in the
anaerobic reactor (0.71%). The relative abundances of Anaerolinea-
ceae and Blastocatella, which could strengthen hydrolysis, also
signiﬁcantly increased in bioﬁlm of the limited aeration reactor
(21.1% and 4.5%) compared to that in the anaerobic reactor (14.1%
and 3.4%).
3.3. Variations of ﬂuorescent organic substances during hydrolysis
In this study, PARAFAC analysis was employed to characterize
changes of ﬂuorescence DOM during hydrolysis process of the
wastewater (Fig. 4). Residual analysis gave evidence of three com-
ponents being adequate for these data. Then, Component A, B and
C, detected at the excitation/emission wavelengths (Ex/Em) of 235/
350 (225, 280)/320 and 250/455 nm (Fig. 4a), were identiﬁed as
aromatic protein-like (Chen et al., 2003; Zheng et al., 2019), tryp-
tophan protein-like (e.g., aromatic amino acids) (An et al., 2017;
Tang et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2018), and fulvic acid-like substances
with aromatic terrestrial structures and macromolecular weight
(Chen et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2018). As illustrated in
Fig. 4bed, the amount of refractory aromatic protein (Component
A) and intractable fulvic acid (Component C) was the main ﬂuo-
rescent substances of DOM, and biodegradable tryptophan protein
(Component B) occupied relatively small proportion. Interestingly,
maximum ﬂuorescent intensity (Fmax) values of Component A, B
and C all decreased with time under different carrier ﬁlling ratios,
temperatures and limited aeration, which had an alike variation
tendency to the COD (Fig. 2).
Fmax of the three components decreased with increasing carrier
ﬁlling ratio from 0 to 60%. For example, at the end of the reaction
(48 h), Fmax of Component A in DOM of the reactor decreased by
242.6, 317.7, and 354.2, while that of Component C decreased by
62.6, 109.7, and 126.1 following the carrier ﬁlling ratio increasing
from 0 to 60%. Fmax of Component A, B and C decreased as tem-
perature increased from 15 C to 35 C, and reduced when using
reactor with limited aeration. The refractory aromatic protein and
intractable fulvic acid were non-biodegradable (Zheng et al., 2019),
which would increase the difﬁculty of biological treatment of the
industrial park wastewater. These ﬁndings are very encouraging,
showing that higher packing carriers, higher temperature and

3.4. NH4þ-N release during hydrolysis
Fig. 5 illustrates effects of the three inﬂuential factors on the
change of NH4þ-N concentration during the hydrolysis process. In
the batch tests, the released NH4þ-N concentrations were signiﬁ-
cantly correlated with COD decrement with correlation coefﬁcients
of 0.967, 0.901 and 0.947 at 0.01 level for Test 1, Test 2 and Test 3
(Table 1). The results conﬁrmed that the release NH4þ-N was
transformed from the nitrogen-containing organic matters through
decomposition (Bi et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017) in accompany
with the progress of the hydrolysis reaction (Lin et al., 2013), and
could also be employed to indicate hydrolysis efﬁciency. Organic
nitrogen exists in wastewater containing compounds such as
partially metabolized protein fragments, humic substances, urea,
amino acids, nucleic acids, low-molecular weight amines, chelating
agents, and et al. (Pehlivanoglu-Mantas and Sedlak, 2008; Zang
et al., 2000). However, some nitrogen-containing organic matters
are difﬁcult to convert into NH4þ-N during hydrolysis process, or to
be degraded directly by heterotrophic bacteria in the subsequent
process (e.g., aeration tank), resulting that TN removal was deﬁ-
cient to fulﬁll the discharge standard in some industrial park
wastewater treatment plants (Pehlivanoglu-Mantas and Sedlak,
2008).
Compared to inﬂuent wastewater, conventional hydrolysis only
released the concentration of NH4þ-N by 2.8 mg/L after 48 h. As
shown in Fig. 5a, the data increased to 5.1 and 8.9 mg/L when the
carrier ﬁlling ratio was raised to 30% and 60%. The concentrations of
released NH4þ-N were 2.7, 4.1 and 6.8 mg/L after 48 h hydrolysis
with 30% carriers at 15, 25 and 35 C (Fig. 5b). It was found that
higher carrier ﬁlling ratio or temperature could bring higher NH4þ-N
production, showing that adding PE carriers or increasing tem-
perature was conducive to the degradation of nitrogen-containing
organic matter. As shown in Fig. 5c, introducing limited oxygen
also increased NH4þ-N release by 15.1% after 48 h hydrolysis
although it might resulted in partial oxidation of NH4þ-N by nitro-
bacteria (Zhang et al., 2017). The total relative abundance of
Nitrospira and Nitrosomonas, accounted for 0.61% of the total mi-
crobes in bioﬁlm of the anaerobic reactor, and then increased to
0.97% in that of the limited aeration reactor (Fig. 1c). The results
suggested that the actual release of NH4þ-N in the limited aeration
reactor was higher than the observed data in Fig. 5c.
The results obtained from this paper implied that the hydrolysis
system with carrier ﬁlling and limited aeration provided an effec-
tive biological pre-treatment method for the chemical industrial
park WWTP to reduce the organic loading and improve the
biodegradability at normal temperature. For the functional bacteria
in charge of hydrolysis, carriers provide a pleasant enough place to
grow

Increasing

strengthened the activity of enzymes and the metabolic capacity of
microorganisms, but it is not economical to raise the temperature
except waste heat is provided in adjacent region. Limited aeration
could prohibit sulfate reduction to a certain degree in hydrolysis
process and save BOD consumption (Wu et al., 2015). The COD
removal efﬁciency and the average BOD5/COD of the wastewater
were both improved under the limited aeration condition at normal
temperature (Figs. 2c and 3c). Packing carriers and limited aeration
should be an appropriate and suitable method for upgrading the
performance of hydrolysis system in the chemical industrial park
WWTP. On the other hand, investigating pollutants degradation
and bacterial evolution by individual fractions prepared in artiﬁcial
wastewater or separated from real wastewater is a very important

4. Conclusions
Packing carriers in hydrolysis tank intensiﬁed the plentifulness
of microbial community and enriched hydrolytic bacteria (Beta-
proteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, Sphingobacteria, Clostridia,
Bacteroidia). Rising carriers ﬁlling ratio increased ﬁrst-order kinetic
constant of hydrolysis from 0.015 to 0.080 h1, and enhanced
biodegradability of COD in the industrial park wastewater. Rising
temperature stimulated enzymatic activity for hydrolysis with Ea of
80.22 kJ/mol. Limited aeration further enriched hydrolytic bacteria,
inhibited sulfate-reducing bacteria and intensiﬁed biodegradability
of organic substances. Variations of ﬂuorescent organic substances
and NH4þ-N release during hydrolysis conﬁrmed that hydrolysis was
strengthened by packing carriers, increasing ﬁlling ratio, enhancing
temperature and introducing limited aeration. Packing carriers and
limited aeration were techno-economic methods for upgrading the
performance of hydrolysis system in the chemical industrial park
WWTP by enriching hydrolytic bacteria and stimulating their
activities.
